reception.text: The proclamation itself drew little controversy: it covered land already reserved, in a lightly settled territory, under a specific act of Congress.
When the bison arrived at Cache in October 1907, the town turned out along with a band of Comanche people, some of whom camped at the corrals on October 20.
reception.source: Elwin R. Sanborn, Zoological Society Bulletin No. 28, pp. 409–10

political_impact.text: Congress appropriated $15,000 to fence the preserve, build sheds and maintain a buffalo herd presented by the New York Zoological Society, the first federal money spent developing land for wildlife.
Work began on a steel-wire fence seven feet six inches high, shelter sheds, a hay barn and flood-gates, and the first year's hay was bought.
With the renaming of the forest reserves as national forests, the preserve became the Wichita Mountains National Forest and Game Preserve.
Fifteen bison from the New York Zoological Park traveled 1,858 miles by rail to Cache, with Forest Service guard Frank Rush riding along to take charge of the herd.
political_impact.source: American Bison Society, First Report (1905–1907), pp. 64–67

legacy.text: The transplanted herd took hold and grew, in one of the first deliberate reintroductions of a native species to its former range in North America.
The Wichita became the template for later big-game refuges, including the National Bison Range in Montana in 1908.

today.name: Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge
today.note: 59,020 acres of mixed-grass prairie and granite uplands; still home to descendants of the 1907 bison herd, along with elk and longhorn cattle.
today.source: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge, About Us

related.note: Roosevelt enlarged the Wichita reserve on May 29, 1906.

later_actions.text: Congress appropriated $15,000 for a fence, sheds and the maintenance of a buffalo herd on the preserve.
Renamed the Wichita Mountains National Forest and Game Preserve when forest reserves became national forests.

uncertain: Whether the Comanche leader Quanah Parker was at Cache when the bison arrived is not known; neither 1907–08 eyewitness account names him.
Current head counts for the refuge's bison, elk and longhorn herds are not published.
